newsitem.title: FRANCE: Moslem rebels kill 93 in Algeria farming community.
newsitem.headline: Moslem rebels kill 93 in Algeria farming community.

text.p: Moslem rebels killed 93 people in an overnight raid on a village south of Algiers, leaving their bodies lying in blood after cutting their throats or hacking them to death with farm implements, Algeria's government said on Tuesday.

The death toll, which included 43 women and girls, was the highest in a single attack on villagers in more than five years of conflict in which Moslem fundamentalist guerrillas have been fighting to try to topple the government.
The Algerian government, inured to bloodshed after a series of village massacres in which nearly 300 people have now died in about two weeks, described the killings as "horrible".
"The attack showed a savagery without any precedent," the government said in its statement carried on state media.

"A band of terrorists attacked the inhabitants of this isolated agricultural community, savagely assassinating with knives and agricultural tools, 93 people, among them 43 women and young girls, and three children," it said.
Another 25 were wounded, including 18 in a serious state.
The death toll was almost double the previous worst attack, early this month, when rebels exterminated all the 52 inhabitants of a village in Medea province, 70 km (45 miles) south of Algiers.
The government said some of those who carried out the attack over Monday-Tuesday had been killed:

"The alert being given in the night enabled security forces to intervene, preventing these criminals from increasing the toll of this assassination and to kill certain elements of this band which is being hunted."
Algerian officials use the term "terrorist" or "criminal" to describe Moslem fundamentalists.
As it has done in the past, it urged people to be vigilant and on their guard against attacks.

The rebels moved into Baouch Boukhelef-Khemisti farming community in Bougara district late on Monday, and the slaughter went on through the night. It took place only 25 km (15 miles) south of the capital Algiers.

Algeria has suffered a series of massacres in villages, particularly since it set a date -- June 5 -- for parliamentary elections to be held. The attack coincided with the deadline for political parties to register their list of candidates to compete in the poll.

The ballot will be the first legislative election to be held since the authorities in January 1992 cancelled a general election in which Moslem fundamentalists had taken a commanding first round lead.
Shortly afterwards, violence erupted and about 60,000 people have since been killed. The conflict initially almost exclusively involved security forces and Moslem guerrillas.

But it spread slowly to relatives of police and soldiers, to tightly censored journalists seen by rebels as supporting the government, to high-profile personalities and to those living in isolated villages and seen as easy targets.
